title: Ceres et Proserpina
titleEn: The Seizing of Proserpina — Metamorphoses V.341–461
source: P. Ovidius Naso, Metamorphoses, ed. Hugo Magnus (Gotha: F.A. Perthes), public domain; TEI from PerseusDL/canonical-latinLit phi0959.phi006.perseus-lat2, sha256 fb3fdb1d8a4a3b82. Collated against The Latin Library (cltk mirror) as a disagreement detector only. Original spelling kept. Pronunciation convention: reconstructed Classical (restored) Latin, applied consistently. All translations were made fresh from the Latin for Lectorium.
about: Ceres' daughter is carried off. The part opens inside a song - which is why the quotation mark at 341 opens and never closes here, and why the voice singing is one standing inside the poem rather than the poet's own - with a hymn to Ceres as the first giver of ploughing, of crops and of law. From there it goes underground: Sicily is described as the weight heaped on the giant Typhoeus, whose struggles shake the island, and it is those tremors that bring Dis up out of the dark to inspect his roof for cracks. Venus, watching from her own mountain, sees him and sets Cupid on him out of policy rather than pity - a third of the world is not yet hers. The arrow strikes; at a lake near Henna, where it is spring all year round, Proserpina is picking flowers with her companions, and she is seen, loved and seized almost in one moment. The chariot runs down through Sicily to the pool of the nymph Cyane, who rises out of her own water to bar the way and tells the god plainly that the girl should have been asked for and not taken; he opens a road to Tartarus with his sceptre and drives through it, and Cyane grieves until she dissolves into the water she had been the divinity of. The last third of the part follows Ceres, searching land and sea by torchlight and by daylight, until she stops at a thatched cottage for a drink and a boy laughs at the way she takes it. This is the first of two parts.

advisory.lede: This part tells the seizing of Proserpina: a girl carried off by force, against her will and her mother's, to be the wife of her father's brother.
advisory.more: The abduction is arranged as policy. Venus sets Cupid on Dis to extend her own power over the third of the world she does not yet hold, and at 378-379 she asks him to 'join the goddess to her uncle' - 'patruus' is precise, a father's brother, and Dis is Jupiter's. Ovid gives the act itself in a single line, 395: Proserpina is seen, loved and seized 'almost in the same moment', the object of all three passive verbs and the agent of none, and the poem's comment on it is that love was in a hurry. Nothing in the Latin gives her a word of her own; she cries out for her mother, and she grieves over her spilled flowers. The nymph Cyane puts the objection at 415-416 - she ought to have been asked for, not seized - and contrasts it with her own marriage, entered into after being asked. From 402 the poem stops naming him in these lines and calls him 'raptor', the noun formed from the verb used of the act. The text is presented unaltered and the translation does not soften it.

sentences.t:
“Prima Ceres unco glaebam dimovit aratro,
prima dedit fruges alimentaque mitia terris,
prima dedit leges: Cereris sunt omnia munus.
sentences.l: First Ceres turned the clod aside with the hooked plough, first gave crops and gentle nourishment to the lands, first gave laws: all things are the gift of Ceres.
sentences.i: Ceres was the first to break the clod with the curved plough, the first to give the earth its crops and its mild food, the first to give it laws: it is all Ceres' gift.
sentences.n: The song opens with a triple 'prima', 'first', standing in the same position in three successive lines - the figure is anaphora, and it is the plainest way Latin verse has of hammering a claim home. 'unco aratro' is an ablative of means, and 'glaebam dimovit', 'moved the clod aside', is the exact motion of a ploughshare rather than a general word for ploughing. In 'Cereris sunt omnia munus' the plural neuter 'omnia' takes the singular 'munus' as its complement: all things are one gift, not many gifts. The line is a sententia, a general truth set down to close the run.

sentences.t: Illa canenda mihi est.
sentences.l: She is to be sung by me.
sentences.i: She is my subject.
sentences.n: 'canenda' is a gerundive, the verbal adjective of obligation, and 'canenda est' with a dative ('mihi') is the standard Latin way of saying 'I must sing her': the person who must act goes into the dative rather than the nominative, so the goddess is the grammatical subject of the sentence and the singer only its agent. Note also that the quotation mark opened at 341 is never closed inside this part - everything here is sung by a speaker standing inside the poem.

sentences.t:
Utinam modo dicere possem
carmina digna dea: certe dea carmine digna est.
sentences.l: If only I could but sing songs worthy of the goddess: certainly the goddess is worthy of a song.
sentences.i: If only I could sing a song worthy of the goddess - and worthy of a song she certainly is.
sentences.n: 'utinam' with the imperfect subjunctive ('possem') is a wish for what is not the case: 'if only I could', with the admission built in that the singer cannot. Magnus prints 'possem'; some editions print 'possim', the present subjunctive, which makes it an open wish rather than an impossible one. 'digna' takes an ablative of the thing deserved, and the phrase is turned inside out from one clause to the next - 'carmina digna dea' becomes 'dea carmine digna' - so that the same two words change places around the verb. 'modo' here is restrictive, 'only, merely' - not the temporal 'lately, just now' the same word carries at 428 and 455, which cannot stand with a wish about the present.

sentences.t:
Vasta giganteis ingesta est insula membris
Trinacris et magnis subiectum molibus urget
aetherias ausum sperare Typhoea sedes.
sentences.l: A vast island, Trinacris, has been heaped upon giant limbs, and it presses down Typhoeus, thrust beneath its great masses, who dared to hope for the seats of heaven.
sentences.i: A vast island, Trinacria, was piled on a giant's limbs, and it holds Typhoeus down, pinned under its great masses, who dared to set his hopes on the halls of heaven.
sentences.n: 'Trinacris' is Sicily, 'the three-cornered', named from the three capes the next lines pin the giant under. 'ingesta est' is the verb for shovelling earth onto something, so the island is a load rather than a lid. 'ausum sperare ... Typhoea' is a participle governing an infinitive, 'Typhoeus, having dared to hope', and 'Typhoea' keeps its Greek accusative ending; the whole accusative phrase is held back so that the giant's name arrives last, after his crime. 'subiectum ... molibus' is 'thrust under the masses', with 'molibus' a dative after the compound verb rather than an ablative of means with 'urget' - the same construction, and the same root, as 'subiecta Peloro' at 350.

sentences.t: Nititur ille quidem pugnatque resurgere saepe,
sentences.l: He, for his part, strains and fights to rise again, often,
sentences.i: He struggles, true enough, and fights again and again to get up,
sentences.n: 'ille quidem' is concessive - 'he does indeed strive' - and the 'sed' at the head of the next line is waiting to cancel it. 'nititur' is deponent, passive in form and active in sense, 'he strains'; 'pugnat resurgere' gives 'pugnare' an infinitive as though it meant 'tries'. The present tenses here and for the next five lines are not narrative presents: this is what the giant is doing now, and permanently.

sentences.t:
dextra sed Ausonio manus est subiecta Peloro,
laeva, Pachyne, tibi, Lilybaeo crura premuntur,
sentences.l: but his right hand has been put under Ausonian Pelorus, his left under you, Pachynus, his legs are pressed by Lilybaeum,
sentences.i: but his right hand lies pinned under Ausonian Pelorus, his left under you, Pachynus, and Lilybaeum weighs down his legs;
sentences.n: The three names are Sicily's three capes: Pelorus in the north-east, facing 'Ausonian' Italy across the strait, Pachynus in the south-east, Lilybaeum in the west. 'laeva' has no noun with it - 'manus', hand, is carried over from the line before and English has to supply it. 'Pachyne, tibi' is an apostrophe: the singer breaks off from the story to speak to a headland directly, and this poem does that to places as readily as to people. Both verbs are passive, 'subiecta est' and 'premuntur', so the giant is what is acted on throughout and never the agent.

sentences.t:
degravat Aetna caput: sub qua resupinus harenas
eiectat flammamque ferox vomit ore Typhoeus.
sentences.l: Etna weighs down his head: under her, lying on his back, savage Typhoeus throws up sand and vomits flame from his mouth.
sentences.i: Etna bears down on his head; under it Typhoeus lies on his back and hurls up sand, and savagely spews flame from his mouth.
sentences.n: 'sub qua' is a connecting relative agreeing with 'Aetna', which is feminine in Latin: 'under which mountain'. Latin uses this trick of opening a clause with a relative constantly, where English would start a new sentence. 'resupinus' is an adjective describing him, 'flat on his back', where English wants a phrase; 'ferox' is another one hung on the giant where the sense is really 'savagely'. This is an aetiology, a story that explains why something in the world is as it is: the eruptions of Etna are one buried body's struggle, and the geography of the whole island has just been laid out to make the picture exact.

sentences.t:
Saepe remoliri luctatur pondera terrae
oppidaque et magnos devolvere corpore montes.
sentences.l: Often he wrestles to heave back the weights of the earth and to roll the towns and the great mountains off his body.
sentences.i: Often he strains to shove the earth's weight back and roll the towns and the great mountains off him.
sentences.n: 'luctatur' is deponent, 'he wrestles', and takes the two infinitives 'remoliri' and 'devolvere' as though it meant 'tries'. 'corpore' is an ablative of separation with 'devolvere', 'to roll down off his body'. 'remoliri' is a rare compound meaning to heave back what has been heaped on. The towns stand in the same list as the mountains, and that is the point: a whole inhabited island is the load.

sentences.t:
Inde tremit tellus, et rex pavet ipse silentum,
ne pateat latoque solum retegatur hiatu
inmissusque dies trepidantes terreat umbras.
sentences.l: From that the earth trembles, and the king of the silent ones himself is afraid, lest the ground gape and be uncovered by a wide chasm, and the daylight let in terrify the trembling shades.
sentences.i: That is why the earth quakes, and the king of the silent ones himself takes fright, in case the ground should split, be laid open by some wide chasm, and the daylight let in should terrify the shivering shades.
sentences.n: 'rex silentum' - 'the king of the silent' - is the poem's name here for Dis, ruler of the dead; 'silentum' is a genitive plural of a participle used as a noun, 'of those who are silent'. 'pavet ne ...' is a fear clause: after a verb of fearing, 'ne' means 'lest', that is, 'that it may happen', which is the reverse of what a negative leads an English reader to expect. All three subjunctives - 'pateat', 'retegatur', 'terreat' - hang from that one 'ne'. 'inmissus dies' is 'the daylight let in', a participle doing the work of a relative clause; the edition prints 'inm-' where later texts print 'imm-', and we keep it.

sentences.t:
Hanc metuens cladem tenebrosa sede tyrannus
exierat, curruque atrorum vectus equorum
ambibat Siculae cautus fundamina terrae.
sentences.l: Fearing this disaster, the monarch had gone out from his shadowy seat and, carried by a chariot of black horses, was going round the foundations of the Sicilian land, cautious.
sentences.i: In fear of that disaster the monarch had come up out of his dark seat, and, drawn by a chariot of black horses, was making a careful circuit of the foundations of Sicily.
sentences.n: 'tyrannus' is a Greek word for a sole ruler and in Latin verse it need carry no blame: here it names Dis by his office, as 'rex silentum' did three lines earlier. 'metuens' takes a plain accusative of the thing feared. 'vectus' is a passive participle, 'having been carried', which is how Latin says 'riding'. 'cautus' is an adjective attached to the man where English would use an adverb, 'cautiously' - and it earns its place, since he is out inspecting his own roof for cracks. The pluperfect 'exierat' sets the journey up and the imperfect 'ambibat' keeps him circling on it.

sentences.t:
Postquam exploratum satis est loca nulla labare,
depositoque metu, videt hunc Erycina vagantem
monte suo residens,
sentences.l: After it had been examined enough that no places were giving way, and with his fear laid aside, Erycina, sitting on her own mountain, sees him wandering,
sentences.i: Once it had been checked well enough that nowhere was giving way, and his fear was laid aside, Erycina, seated on her own mountain, saw him roaming there,
sentences.n: 'exploratum satis est' is an impersonal passive - 'it has been searched out enough' - with nobody named as the searcher, and it governs the indirect statement 'loca nulla labare', 'that no places are giving way'. 'deposito metu' is an ablative absolute, 'the fear having been put down', a self-contained phrase where English wants a clause; this construction is everywhere in Latin verse and is worth learning to hear as a clause. 'videt' is a present dropped into a past narrative - the historic present, which this poem switches in and out of constantly. 'Erycina' is Venus, named from her temple on Mount Eryx in western Sicily, so 'monte suo', 'on her own mountain', means she is watching from her own sanctuary and the scene never leaves the island.

sentences.t:
natumque amplexa volucrem
“arma manusque meae, mea, nate, potentia”, dixit,
“illa, quibus superas omnes, cape tela, Cupido,
sentences.l: and having embraced her winged son, 'my weapons and my hands, my power, son,' she said, 'take up those shafts, Cupid, with which you overcome all,
sentences.i: and putting her arms round her winged son she said: 'My arms, my hands, my power, my boy - take up those shafts of yours, Cupid, that you conquer everyone with,
sentences.n: 'amplexa' is the perfect participle of a deponent verb, so it is active in meaning, 'having embraced', although passive in form. The string 'arma manusque meae, mea ... potentia' stands in apposition to 'tela' in the next line, the object of 'cape': she calls the arrows her weapons, her hands and her power before she says what they are. 'nate', the vocative 'son', is dropped inside that phrase, and Cupid's own name waits to the end of the following line. 'arma' is equipment for fighting and 'manus' is the hand as the thing that does a deed, so neither word is as flat as it looks.

sentences.t:
inque dei pectus celeres molire sagittas,
cui triplicis cessit fortuna novissima regni.
sentences.l: and drive your swift arrows into the breast of the god to whom the last lot of the threefold kingdom fell.
sentences.i: and drive your swift arrows into the breast of the god who drew the last lot of the threefold realm.
sentences.n: 'molire' is the imperative of the deponent 'molior', 'set in motion, heave' - a heavy word for launching an arrow, and it makes the shot an act of engineering. 'cui ... cessit' is a relative clause with a dative: a thing 'falls to' a person in Latin as in English. The threefold kingdom is the world divided by lot between three brothers - sky, sea and the dead - and 'fortuna novissima' is the lot that came out last, 'novissimus', literally 'newest', being the ordinary Latin word for 'last'. In this whole speech Venus never names him: he is 'the god' here and simply 'her uncle' at 379.

sentences.t:
Tu superos ipsumque Iovem tu numina ponti
victa domas ipsumque, regit qui numina ponti.
sentences.l: You tame the gods above and Jupiter himself, you tame the divinities of the sea, conquered, and himself who rules the divinities of the sea.
sentences.i: You master the gods above and Jupiter himself; you master the powers of the sea, beaten, and the very god who rules the powers of the sea.
sentences.n: 'victa' is a participle agreeing with 'numina' and standing predicatively: he tames them 'as conquered', that is, he conquers them and then holds them. The line ends on the same two words the line before ended on, 'numina ponti', with the god who rules them added at the second turn; the repetition is a figure deliberately built, not a fault in the text. The doubled 'Tu ... tu' at the front is anaphora again, as at 341-343. 'superos' is an adjective used as a noun, 'those above', the standing word for the gods of heaven.

sentences.t:
Tartara quid cessant? cur non matrisque tuumque
imperium profers? agitur pars tertia mundi.
sentences.l: Why does Tartarus hold off? Why do you not extend your mother's rule and your own? A third part of the world is at stake.
sentences.i: Why is Tartarus left alone? Why not push your mother's empire and your own out that far? A third of the world is at stake.
sentences.n: 'Tartara' is a neuter plural used of a single place, so it takes a plural verb where English says 'Tartarus is'. 'cessant' is 'hold off, stand idle': the question is why that one region has been let alone. 'matrisque tuumque' pairs a genitive noun with a possessive adjective - Latin allows the mismatch and English has to even it out. 'agitur' is the language of the lawcourt and the wager: the thing 'is being dealt with', that is, is at risk, the same idiom as 'res agitur', 'the matter is at stake'.

sentences.t:
Et tamen in caelo, quae iam patientia nostra est,
spernimur, ac mecum vires minuuntur Amoris.
sentences.l: And yet in heaven - what patience of ours it is by now - we are scorned, and along with me the strength of Love is being lessened.
sentences.i: And even in heaven - such is the patience we have come to - we are treated with contempt, and Love's power dwindles along with mine.
sentences.n: 'quae iam patientia nostra est' is a parenthesis built on an exclamatory relative: 'what patience of ours it is!', that is, 'see how much we put up with'. 'spernimur' is first person plural passive, 'we are scorned': in the scorn Venus speaks for herself and her son together. The clause that follows separates them again - 'mecum' is singular, 'along with me' - and sets Love's strength beside her own rather than inside it. 'Amoris' is Cupid himself, named by the noun 'love', so mother and son are one power and a slight to her is a loss of strength in him.

sentences.t:
Pallada nonne vides iaculatricemque Dianam
abscessisse mihi?
sentences.l: Do you not see that Pallas and javelin-throwing Diana have withdrawn from me?
sentences.i: Do you not see that Pallas and Diana of the javelin have got clear of me?
sentences.n: 'Pallada' is a Greek accusative of the name Pallas, kept as the edition prints it. 'nonne' asks a question that expects the answer yes. Both goddesses stand in the accusative as the subject of the infinitive 'abscessisse' - indirect statement after 'vides', 'you see that they have withdrawn'. 'mihi' is a dative of the person concerned, 'from me' in the sense of 'to my loss'. Both goddesses are unmarried, and that is what Venus is counting as a defection.

sentences.t:
Cereris quoque filia virgo,
si patiemur, erit: nam spes adfectat easdem.
sentences.l: Ceres' daughter too will be a virgin, if we allow it: for she reaches after the same hopes.
sentences.i: Ceres' daughter will be a virgin too, if we let her: her ambitions run the same way.
sentences.n: 'quoque' here is the plain adverb 'too'. Be warned that the same shape is often 'quo-que', 'and with which', and telling the two apart is a running task in this poem; it comes back as the adverb at 401 and 411. 'virgo erit' is 'she will be an unmarried girl', that is, she will stay one. 'patiemur' is future indicative, not subjunctive: 'if we shall allow it'. 'spes ... easdem', 'the same hopes', means the same hopes as Pallas and Diana in the line before.

sentences.t:
At tu, pro socio, siqua est ea gratia, regno
iunge deam patruo.”
sentences.l: But you - in return for our shared kingdom, if that favour counts for anything - join the goddess to her uncle.'
sentences.i: But you, for the sake of the realm we share - if that counts for anything with you - marry the goddess to her uncle.'
sentences.n: 'pro socio ... regno' is split by the parenthesis 'siqua est ea gratia', so the noun and its adjective sit on either side of the aside: 'for the partnership in rule', the joint sway of mother and son that the whole speech has been claiming. 'gratia' is the return owed for a favour, the currency of Roman obligation. 'iunge' is the verb for marrying someone off, taking a dative of the man; 'patruo' is exact - a father's brother, not a mother's - so what Venus is arranging is a marriage between Proserpina and her father's brother, and the girl is the object of the verb throughout. See this part's advisory.

sentences.t:
Dixit Venus. Ille pharetram
solvit et arbitrio matris de mille sagittis
unam seposuit,
sentences.l: Venus spoke. He loosed his quiver and, at his mother's discretion, set apart one arrow out of a thousand,
sentences.i: So Venus spoke. He unfastened his quiver and, as his mother directed, picked one arrow out of a thousand,
sentences.n: 'arbitrio matris' is an ablative, 'by his mother's judgement': the choice of the arrow is hers and not his, which is how the speech is answered without a word of reply. 'de mille sagittis unam' uses 'de' for the partitive, 'one out of a thousand', where Latin might equally have used a genitive. 'seposuit' is the everyday word for putting a thing by, used here of selecting a weapon.

sentences.t:
sed qua nec acutior ulla
nec minus incerta est nec quae magis audiat arcus,
sentences.l: but one than which none is sharper, none less uncertain, and none that obeys the bow more,
sentences.i: but one with nothing sharper than it, nothing surer, nothing that answers the bow better -
sentences.n: 'qua' is an ablative of comparison, 'than which', and it governs all three limbs of the sentence. 'nec minus incerta' is litotes, a negative standing in for an emphatic positive: 'nor is any less unsure than it' means that it is the surest of them all, and English needs the positive to keep the force. 'quae magis audiat' is subjunctive because it describes the kind of arrow this is rather than recording a fact about it. 'audire' is 'to listen to' and so 'to obey', which is exactly what an arrow does to a bowstring.

sentences.t:
oppositoque genu curvavit flexile cornum
inque cor hamata percussit harundine Ditem.
sentences.l: and with his knee set against it he bent the pliant horn and struck Dis to the heart with the barbed reed.
sentences.i: and setting his knee against it he bent the springy bow and struck Dis to the heart with the barbed shaft.
sentences.n: 'opposito genu' is an ablative absolute, 'the knee having been set against it', and it describes the ordinary way of bending a bow to string or draw it. 'cornum' is horn, the material, standing for the bow made of it, and 'harundine' is a reed standing for the arrow shafted with it: a thing named by what it is made of, twice in two lines. In the last line 'hamata ... harundine' is split around the verb it belongs to, and the god's name is held back to the final word, so the reader learns where the arrow lands before learning who is hit.

sentences.t:
Haud procul Hennaeis lacus est a moenibus altae,
nomine Pergus, aquae.
sentences.l: Not far from the walls of Henna there is a lake of deep water, Pergus by name.
sentences.i: Not far from the walls of Henna lies a lake of deep water, Pergus by name.
sentences.n: 'altae ... aquae' is a genitive of description, 'of deep water', with the adjective at the end of one line and its noun in the middle of the next and the rest of the sentence in between - a stretch worth expecting rather than puzzling over. 'nomine' is an ablative of respect, 'in respect of its name'. Henna stood in the middle of Sicily and its cult of Ceres was famous, so the scene is set at the island's centre, as far from any coast as the poem could put it.

sentences.t:
Non illo plura Caystros
carmina cycnorum labentibus audit in undis.
sentences.l: Not more songs of swans does the Cayster hear on its gliding waters than that lake does.
sentences.i: The Cayster hears no more swan-song on its gliding water than that lake does.
sentences.n: 'illo' is an ablative of comparison, 'than it', standing for the lake, and the comparison is carried by 'plura', 'more', with the two words pulled apart to opposite ends of the phrase. The Cayster is a river in Lydia proverbial for its swans, so the line sets a small Sicilian pool against the most famous swan-water there was. 'labentibus in undis' is 'in' with the ablative of place, 'on the gliding waters', with the preposition wedged inside the phrase it governs.

sentences.t:
Silva coronat aquas cingens latus omne, suisque
frondibus ut velo Phoebeos submovet ictus.
sentences.l: A wood crowns the waters, circling every side, and with its own leaves, as with an awning, it keeps off the strokes of Phoebus.
sentences.i: A wood rings the water, circling it on every side, and with its leaves for an awning it keeps the sun's stroke off.
sentences.n: 'ut velo' is 'as with a sail-cloth': the 'velum' was the awning stretched over a theatre or a courtyard to keep the sun off an audience, so the image is of a made shade rather than of shadow in general. 'Phoebeos ictus', 'the blows of Phoebus', names the sun-god for his light, and 'ictus' treats sunlight as something that strikes. 'coronat' and 'cingens' say the same thing twice over, once as a verb and once as a participle, which is how the line closes the circle it is describing.

sentences.t:
Frigora dant rami, tyrios humus umida flores:
perpetuum ver est.
sentences.l: The branches give coolness, the moist ground gives Tyrian flowers: it is spring without end.
sentences.i: The branches give cool shade, the damp ground purple flowers; it is spring the whole year round.
sentences.n: The second clause has no verb of its own: 'dant' is made to serve twice, once for the branches and once for the ground, and Latin leaves the reader to carry it across. 'tyrios' is the deep red-purple of the dye made at Tyre, the costliest colour in the Roman world, used here of wild flowers. 'perpetuum ver est' is three words and a whole climate: the place stands outside the seasons, which is what makes what happens in it possible.

sentences.t:
Quo dum Proserpina luco
ludit et aut violas aut candida lilia carpit,
dumque puellari studio calathosque sinumque
implet et aequales certat superare legendo,
sentences.l: While Proserpina is playing in that grove and picking now violets, now white lilies, and while with girlish eagerness she fills her baskets and the fold of her dress and strives to outdo the girls of her own age in the gathering,
sentences.i: While Proserpina was playing in that grove, picking violets or white lilies, and with a girl's eagerness filling her baskets and the fold of her dress, trying to gather more than the girls of her own age,
sentences.n: 'Quo ... luco' is a connecting relative with its noun inside its own clause, 'in which grove': Latin uses this to stitch one sentence to the last, and it comes again at 413. 'dum' with a present indicative regularly means 'while' of past time, which is why the idiomatic English goes into the past although the Latin does not. 'calathos' are the wicker baskets used for flowers and for wool; 'sinum' is the fold of the dress gathered up to carry things in, the pocket of ancient dress. 'legendo' is a gerund in the ablative, 'by picking', and 'aequales' are girls of the same age - the whole picture is a game with a score in it.

sentences.t:
paene simul visa est dilectaque raptaque Diti:
usque adeo est properatus amor.
sentences.l: almost in the same moment she was seen, and loved, and seized by Dis: so hurried was his love.
sentences.i: she was seen, loved and seized by Dis almost in one moment - his love was in that much haste.
sentences.n: Three passive verbs share one subject and one agent: 'visa est, dilecta [est], rapta [est] Diti', with 'Diti' a dative of agent, a construction Latin allows with the perfect passive and verse uses freely where prose would say 'a Dite'. She is the object of all three - seen, loved, seized - and does nothing at all in the sentence; the grammar carries the whole event. 'paene simul' is 'almost at the same time', and the two '-que' endings run the three acts together without a pause between them. 'properatus' is a participle used as a predicate, 'made hasty': the last four words are the poem's own comment on what it has just told, and 'amor', love, is the word it chooses for it. See this part's advisory.

sentences.l: The terrified goddess calls, with sorrowing mouth, on both her mother and her companions, but on her mother more often;
sentences.i: In terror the goddess cries out for her mother and for her companions - but for her mother more often -
sentences.n: 'clamat' takes a plain accusative of the person called on, which English has to render as 'calls for' or 'calls on'. 'maesto ... ore' is an ablative of means wrapped right around the following line, with the correction 'sed matrem saepius' dropped inside it: the poem stops in the middle of its own phrase to say which name came oftener. 'et ... et' is 'both ... and'. She is 'Dea', the goddess, not 'the girl': the word makes no difference to what is happening to her, and that is part of the point.

sentences.t:
et, ut summa vestem laniarat ab ora,
conlecti flores tunicis cecidere remissis.
sentences.l: and, since she had torn her dress from its topmost edge, the gathered flowers fell as the loosened tunic let them go.
sentences.i: and, because she had torn her dress down from the top edge, the flowers she had gathered fell out of the loosened tunic.
sentences.n: 'cecidere' is 'ceciderunt', the poetic third-person plural perfect in '-ere'. It is everywhere in hexameter and is often the first thing that makes a line look strange, so it is worth fixing now: any '-ere' where the sense wants a past may be one of these. 'laniarat' is a syncopated pluperfect for 'laniaverat', with the '-ve-' dropped, another verse habit. 'tunicis remissis' is an ablative absolute, 'the tunic having been let go'. The detail is exact and pitiless: she tore her own dress in the struggle, and that is why the fold she was carrying the flowers in came open.

sentences.t:
Tantaque simplicitas puerilibus adfuit annis,
haec quoque virgineum movit iactura dolorem.
sentences.l: And so great a simplicity belonged to her childish years that this loss too stirred a girl's grief.
sentences.i: And her childish years had such innocence in them that even this loss brought her a girl's grief.
sentences.n: 'tanta ...' sets up a result clause whose 'ut' is simply left out, so the two statements are set side by side and the reader supplies 'that'. 'quoque' is the adverb 'too' again, and the whole weight of the sentence rests on it: after everything in the last five lines, the spilled flowers are still worth crying over. 'iactura' is a merchant's word, the loss of goods thrown overboard to save a ship. 'puerilibus annis' is a dative with 'adfuit', 'was present to her childish years'.

sentences.t:
Raptor agit currus et nomine quemque vocando
exhortatur equos, quorum per colla iubasque
excutit obscura tinctas ferrugine habenas,
sentences.l: The ravisher drives his chariot and urges on the horses, calling each by name, and over their necks and manes he shakes out the reins dyed with dark rust-colour,
sentences.i: The ravisher drives his chariot on, urging the horses, calling each of them by name, and shakes the reins - dyed a dark rust-colour - out over their necks and manes,
sentences.n: 'Raptor' is the poem's own noun for him here: 'the one who seizes', formed straight from the verb 'rapere' used of the act seven lines earlier at 395. From this point to the end of the part his name is not used again - he is 'Raptor' here and 'Saturnius', the son of Saturn, at 420. 'nomine quemque vocando' is a gerund in the ablative, 'by calling each by name'. 'ferrugo' is the dark colour of iron-rust, a blue-black rather than the orange English means by rust, and it is the standing colour of the underworld's gear. 'obscura ... ferrugine' is wrapped around 'tinctas', which agrees with 'habenas' at the end of the line.

sentences.t:
perque lacus altos et olentia sulphure fertur
stagna Palicorum, rupta fervenu terra,
sentences.l: and he is carried past deep lakes and the pools of the Palici, which stink of sulphur and [boil?] where the earth has burst,
sentences.i: and he is swept on past deep lakes and the sulphur-stinking pools of the Palici, [boiling?] where the earth has broken open,
sentences.n: The digitization of the archived edition is damaged here, in a single word: 'fervenu' is not a Latin word, and the line will not scan as it stands - it is a syllable short of what the hexameter needs, and the token standing in the gap has no quantities to measure. What both the sense and the metre require is 'ferventia', 'boiling', a neuter plural participle agreeing with 'stagna' and running parallel to 'olentia' in the line before - the pools of the Palici are volcanic and were famous for bubbling. The word is left exactly as the archive has it and the translation marks the gap with brackets rather than quietly filling it. 'rupta ... terra' is an ablative absolute, 'the earth having burst'. The Palici were twin gods of those pools in eastern Sicily, and an oath sworn at them was the most binding oath on the island.

sentences.t:
et qua Bacchiadae, bimari gens orta Corintho,
inter inaequales posuerunt moenia portus.
sentences.l: and where the Bacchiadae, a race sprung from two-sea'd Corinth, set walls between unequal harbours.
sentences.i: and past the place where the Bacchiadae, a people out of Corinth of the two seas, built their walls between two unequal harbours.
sentences.n: 'qua' is 'where', an adverbial relative with nothing to agree with, and it still hangs from 'fertur' in the line before: the chariot is being carried past place after place. 'bimari Corintho' is 'Corinth of the two seas' - the city sits on the isthmus with a gulf on either side - and 'orta' is a participle taking an ablative of origin. The Bacchiadae were the clan that ruled Corinth and were driven out of it; the city they founded between the unequal harbours is Syracuse. 'posuerunt' is the full third-person plural perfect where the poem often prints '-ere', as at 399.

sentences.t:
Est medium Cyanes et Pisaeae Arethusae,
quod coit angustis inclusum cornibus aequor.
sentences.l: There is a stretch of water midway between Cyane and Pisaean Arethusa, which draws together, shut in by narrow horns of land.
sentences.i: There is a stretch of water midway between Cyane and Pisaean Arethusa, closing in on itself, penned between narrow horns of land.
sentences.n: The subject 'aequor' is held back to the very last word, with its adjective 'medium' at the head of the sentence and a relative clause in between: the sentence is built to make you wait, and reading it means holding 'medium' unattached for a line and a half. 'Cyanes' is a Greek genitive of the name Cyane, and 'Pisaeae' calls the spring Arethusa 'of Pisa', the town in Elis in Greece from which she was said to have come. 'cornibus', horns, is the standing word for the two arms of land that close a bay.

sentences.t:
Hic fuit, a cuius stagnum quoque nomine dictum est,
inter Sicelidas Cyane celeberrima nymphas.
sentences.l: Here lived Cyane, most renowned among the nymphs of Sicily, from whose name the pool too is called.
sentences.i: Here lived Cyane, the most famous of the nymphs of Sicily; the pool is named after her as well.
sentences.n: 'Hic' is the adverb 'here', not the pronoun 'this man' - the two are spelt alike and told apart only by sense. 'quoque' is the adverb 'too' once more, and it does real work: the water and the nymph carry one name, which is what makes the end of her story legible when it comes. 'Sicelidas' is a Greek accusative plural, 'Sicilian', kept in its Greek form. 'celeberrima' is the superlative of 'celeber', much frequented and so much spoken of.

sentences.t:
Gurgite quae medio summa tenus exstitit alvo
agnovitque deam.
sentences.l: And she rose out of the middle of the pool as far as the top of her belly and recognised the goddess.
sentences.i: She rose from mid-pool, out as far as the waist, and knew the goddess.
sentences.n: 'quae' opens the sentence: a connecting relative, 'and she', the same trick as 'Quo ... luco' at 391. 'tenus' is a postposition and follows its ablative, 'summa ... alvo', 'as far as the top of the belly' - and that ablative is split across the whole line, with two words wedged between the adjective and its noun. 'exstitit' is 'stood out from', of something rising clear of a surface; the edition keeps the older spelling 'exst-'. The goddess she recognises is Proserpina, the accusative object: it is the girl she knows, not the god.

sentences.t:
“Nec longius ibitis!” inquit,
“non potes invitae Cereris gener esse: roganda,
non rapienda fuit.
sentences.l: 'You shall go no further!' she said. 'You cannot be the son-in-law of an unwilling Ceres: she ought to have been asked for, not seized.
sentences.i: 'You shall go no further!' she said. 'You cannot be son-in-law to a Ceres who is unwilling. She should have been asked for, not seized.
sentences.n: 'ibitis' is plural: with one word she blocks the pair of them, the god and the girl he is carrying. 'invitae Cereris gener' packs the whole objection into a single genitive phrase - a man cannot be another's son-in-law against the mother's will, and Roman marriage did in fact require the consent of the family. 'roganda ... rapienda fuit' is two gerundives with 'fuit', the construction for an obligation that was not met: 'she was one who had to be asked for, not one to be seized'. The two words are chosen for their likeness, 'rogare' against 'rapere', and the judgement of the whole episode is in that pair. See this part's advisory.

sentences.t:
Quodsi componere magnis
parva mihi fas est, et me dilexit Anapis:
exorata tamen, nec, ut haec, exterrita nupsi.”
sentences.l: But if it is right for me to compare small things with great, Anapis too loved me: yet I married won over by entreaty, and not, as she has been, terrified into it.'
sentences.i: And if I may compare small things with great, Anapis loved me too - but I married because I was asked and won over, not, like this girl, terrified into it.'
sentences.n: 'componere magnis parva', to set small things beside great, is the standing formula of a speaker apologising for putting her own case next to a greater one; the small case is her own marriage. 'fas est' is what divine law allows, a stronger word than 'licet'. The Anapus is the river that joins the pool of Cyane near Syracuse, so her marriage is the meeting of two waters. The last line answers the two gerundives of the line before word for word: 'exorata' is 'won over by asking', the passive of what 'roganda' demanded, and 'exterrita' is what 'rapienda' produced. 'ut haec', 'as this one here', points at Proserpina, still in the chariot in front of her.

sentences.t:
Dixit et in partes diversas bracchia tendens
obstitit.
sentences.l: She spoke, and stretching her arms out in opposite directions she stood in the way.
sentences.i: She spoke, and spread her arms wide to either side to block the way.
sentences.n: 'in partes diversas' is 'in different directions', which here means one arm each way, the whole span of the pool: the gesture is the barrier, and it is all she has. 'tendens' is a present participle where English wants a second main verb. 'obstitit', 'stood against', is a compound of 'stare' and normally takes a dative of the person opposed; here it has no object at all, and the standing itself is the act.

sentences.t:
Haud ultra tenuit Saturnius iram,
terribilesque hortatus equos in gurgitis ima
contortum valido sceptrum regale lacerto
condidit.
sentences.l: The son of Saturn held his anger back no further, and, urging on his terrible horses, he buried his royal sceptre, whirled with his powerful arm, in the depths of the pool.
sentences.i: The son of Saturn held his anger no longer: he called his terrible horses on, and with a heave of his powerful arm drove his royal sceptre deep into the pool.
sentences.n: 'Saturnius' is 'the son of Saturn', a patronymic standing in place of a name: Dis, Jupiter and Neptune are all Saturn's sons, and the poem picks the title that puts him among his brothers. 'hortatus' is a deponent participle, active in meaning, 'having urged on'. 'contortum ... lacerto' is a participle with an ablative of means, 'whirled with his strong arm', wrapped around the sceptre it belongs to so that the whole line turns on itself. 'in gurgitis ima' is 'into the deepest parts of the pool', a neuter plural adjective used as a noun. 'condidit' is the verb for burying a sword in a body, and the main verb waits until the first word of the fourth line: the emblem of his kingship is used here as a weapon.

sentences.t:
Icta viam tellus in Tartara fecit
et pronos currus medio cratere recepit.
sentences.l: The struck earth made a way into Tartarus and took in the plunging chariot in the middle of the basin.
sentences.i: The earth, struck, opened a road into Tartarus and received the plunging chariot into the middle of the crater.
sentences.n: 'Icta' is a single participle carrying a whole clause, 'having been struck'. 'viam facere' is the fixed phrase for making a road, and it is chosen coldly: what the blow opens is a route. 'crater' is a Greek loan-word for a mixing-bowl, used of any bowl-shaped hollow - here the hole the sceptre has just made. 'pronos' describes the chariot as tilted forward, going down nose-first, and that is the last we see of it.

sentences.t:
At Cyane, raptamque deam contemptaque fontis
iura sui maerens, inconsolabile vulnus
mente gerit tacita lacrimisque absumitur omnis,
sentences.l: But Cyane, grieving both for the goddess seized and for the rights of her own spring despised, carries an inconsolable wound in her silent mind and, all of her, is used up in tears,
sentences.i: But Cyane, grieving for the goddess carried off and for the scorned rights of her own spring, carries an inconsolable wound in her silent mind and is used up, all of her, in tears,
sentences.n: 'maerens' takes plain accusative objects, and each of them is a noun with a participle doing the work of a whole clause: 'raptam deam' is 'that the goddess was seized', 'contempta iura' is 'that her rights were scorned'. The rights of her spring are a host's rights - a god has driven through her water without asking, as he took the girl without asking - and the two wrongs are put in one grammatical breath. 'omnis' is nominative and agrees with Cyane herself, 'all of her', not with her tears; it is placed last, so the sentence ends on the totality of what is happening to her. 'absumitur lacrimis' is already the transformation, told first as a figure of speech.

sentences.l: and into those waters, of which she had lately been the great divinity, she is thinned away. You would see her limbs soften, her bones suffer bending, her nails lay aside their hardness;
sentences.i: and she is thinned away into the very waters whose great divinity she had been a moment before. You could see the limbs soften, the bones give to bending, the nails lose their hardness;
sentences.n: This is not a damaged word but two whole lines standing in the wrong order in this digitization of the edition: 'ossa pati flexus, ungues posuisse rigorem' belongs after 'Molliri membra videres', not before 'extenuatur aquas', and other editions print the pair the other way round, which is the order the sense requires. As it stands, 'in illas' at the end of 428 is left hanging with no noun to agree with until 'aquas' arrives a line further on and across a semicolon, and two of the three infinitives 'videres' governs now stand ahead of it instead of after it, on the far side of a full stop. The Latin above is left exactly as the archive has it, and the translation follows the order the sense requires. On the grammar: 'quarum' is a relative reaching forward to 'illas ... aquas', and 'in illas ... aquas' is the goal of 'extenuatur', 'she is thinned out into them'. 'videres' is a potential subjunctive addressed to the reader, 'you would see' - of a scene already past, so 'you would have seen' does the same work - and it governs three infinitives in indirect statement, 'molliri', 'pati', 'posuisse', with the perfect 'posuisse' marking the one change already complete.

sentences.t:
primaque de tota tenuissima quaeque liquescunt,
caerulei crines digitique et crura pedesque:
sentences.l: and first out of the whole of her all the slenderest parts melt: her sea-blue hair, and her fingers and legs and feet:
sentences.i: First of the whole of her, every thinnest part melts - the sea-blue hair, the fingers, the legs, the feet;
sentences.n: 'tenuissima quaeque' is 'quisque' with a superlative, the Latin way of saying 'all the thinnest ones'; 'de tota' is 'out of the whole [of her]', with the noun left to be understood from her. 'prima' is a nominative adjective doing adverbial work, 'first'. 'caerulei' is the dark blue-green of the sea, the standing colour of water-divinities, so her hair was already the colour of what she is becoming. The melting runs inward from the extremities - hair, fingers, legs, feet - and the next lines keep that order.

sentences.t:
nam brevis in gelidas membris exilibus undas
transitus est:
sentences.l: for the crossing into cold waters is short for slender limbs:
sentences.i: for slender limbs it is only a short step into cold water.
sentences.n: 'membris exilibus' is a dative of the thing concerned, 'for slender limbs'. 'brevis ... transitus est' is split by everything the crossing has to pass between, so the sentence puts the whole distance inside the phrase that calls it short. 'transitus' is a plain word for a passage or a crossing over. The line is offered as a reason - 'nam', 'for' - as though the dissolution were a matter of physics rather than of grief.

sentences.t:
post haec umeri tergusque latusque
pectoraque in tenues abeunt evanida rivos.
sentences.l: after these her shoulders and back and side and breast, vanishing, pass away into thin streams.
sentences.i: after these her shoulders, her back, her side and her breast fade and pass off into thin streams.
sentences.n: The three '-que' endings in a row are epic polysyndeton, 'and ... and ... and', piling the parts of the body up faster than the sentence can dispose of them. 'tergus' is the back, in the neuter form of the word. 'evanida' is neuter plural, the form Latin uses for a mixed list of things, so it covers the whole run of parts and not just the last of them; it means 'fading out of sight'; 'in ... rivos abeunt' is 'go off into streams', the ordinary verb for going away, used here of a body leaving itself.

sentences.t:
Denique pro vivo vitiatas sanguine venas
lympha subit, restatque nihil, quod prendere possis.
sentences.l: At last, in place of living blood, clear water enters the spoiled veins, and there remains nothing that you could take hold of.
sentences.i: At last clear water comes into the ruined veins in place of living blood, and nothing is left that you could take hold of.
sentences.n: 'pro vivo ... sanguine' is 'instead of living blood', with the noun and its adjective split around 'vitiatas', which belongs to 'venas': the two phrases are interwoven, which is normal in this metre and worth untangling word by word. 'subit' is 'goes up under', the verb for something entering from below and taking a place. 'quod prendere possis' is a relative clause of characteristic with a second-person subjunctive, 'nothing of the sort that you could grasp': the reader is addressed again, as at 'videres' a few lines above, and what she has lost is defined by what a hand would now find.

sentences.t:
Interea pavidae nequiquam filia matri
omnibus est terris, omni quaesita profundo.
sentences.l: Meanwhile the daughter was sought in vain by her frightened mother over all lands and all the deep.
sentences.i: Meanwhile her frightened mother searched for the daughter in vain, over every land and every sea.
sentences.n: 'pavidae ... matri' is a dative of agent with the perfect passive 'quaesita est': the perfect passive freely takes a dative of the agent in verse where prose would use 'a' with the ablative, and a reader who takes 'matri' as 'to her mother' will lose the sentence. The mother is Ceres. 'omnibus ... terris, omni ... profundo' are ablatives of place with no preposition, a licence of verse; 'profundum' is the deep, that is, the sea. 'nequiquam', 'for nothing', is set early in the line, so the failure is known before the search is described.

sentences.t:
Illam non udis veniens Aurora capillis
cessantem vidit, non Hesperus.
sentences.l: Dawn, coming with wet hair, did not see her resting, nor did the Evening Star.
sentences.i: Dawn coming with dew-wet hair never saw her rest, nor did the Evening Star.
sentences.n: 'udis ... capillis' is an ablative of description, 'with wet hair': Dawn's hair is wet with the dew she brings. 'cessantem' agrees with 'Illam' and is predicative - not 'saw her, who was resting', but 'saw her resting', which is the whole point of the line, since she never did. Aurora rises at one end of the day and Hesperus is the star at the other, so the pair between them cover the whole of it.

sentences.t:
Illa duabus
flammiferas pinus manibus succendit ab Aetna
perque pruinosas tulit inrequieta tenebras.
sentences.l: She kindled flame-bearing pines, in her two hands, from Etna, and carried them, unresting, through the frosty darkness.
sentences.i: She lit flame-bearing pine torches at Etna, one in either hand, and carried them unresting through the frosty dark.
sentences.n: 'duabus ... manibus' is an ablative of means split across the line-end with the torches wedged inside it: two hands, two torches, and the arrangement of the words puts one in each. 'pinus' is the pine-tree standing for the torch cut from it, since resinous pine was what torches were made of. 'ab Aetna' is 'from Etna', the mountain that has lain on Typhoeus since 352: she lights her search at the giant's own fire. 'inrequieta' is a nominative adjective where English wants an adverb, 'without rest'; the edition prints 'inr-' where later texts print 'irr-'.

sentences.t:
Rursus ubi alma dies hebetarat sidera, natam
solis ab occasu solis quaerebat ad ortus.
sentences.l: Again, when the kindly day had dulled the stars, she went on seeking her daughter from the sun's setting to the sun's rising.
sentences.i: And again, when the kindly daylight had dimmed the stars, she went on searching for her daughter from sunset to sunrise.
sentences.n: 'hebetarat' is a syncopated pluperfect for 'hebetaverat', with the '-ve-' dropped, as 'laniarat' was at 398. 'alma' is the adjective of nourishing kindness, used of daylight and of Ceres herself. 'solis ab occasu solis ... ad ortus' repeats 'solis' on either side of the line's middle and frames the whole day between the two prepositions; it means from west to east as much as from evening to morning. Set beside the torches of the night before, the line leaves her no hour off. 'quaerebat' is imperfect: the searching goes on and on rather than being done.

sentences.t:
Fessa labore sitim conlegerat oraque nulli
colluerant fontes;
sentences.l: Worn out by her labour she had gathered thirst, and no springs had washed her mouth;
sentences.i: Worn out with the effort she had built up a thirst, and no spring had rinsed her mouth;
sentences.n: 'sitim conligere' is 'to collect thirst', the Latin idiom for growing thirsty: the thirst accumulates like something gathered up along the way. 'ora colluerant fontes' makes the springs the subject and her mouth the object - 'no springs had rinsed her mouth' - where English would rather say she had drunk at none; 'nulli' is nominative plural agreeing with 'fontes'. Magnus prints 'conlegerat', 'had gathered'; some editions print 'conceperat', 'had conceived', with much the same sense. The edition's 'conl-' and 'coll-' spellings are kept as it prints them.

sentences.t:
cum tectam stramine vidit
forte casam parvasque fores pulsavit:
sentences.l: when by chance she saw a cottage roofed with straw and knocked at its small doors:
sentences.i: when by chance she caught sight of a cottage thatched with straw, and knocked at its little door.
sentences.n: 'cum ... vidit' is an inverted cum-clause: the 'when' clause carries the new event rather than the background, and English does the same work with a dash or a full stop. 'tectam stramine ... casam' is a participle with an ablative of means, 'covered with straw', and the noun waits until the next line, so the roof is described before the house it is on. 'fores' is a plural for a single set of double doors; 'casa' is a hut rather than a house, and 'parvas' is one of several words holding the scale of the place down.

sentences.t:
at inde
prodit anus divamque videt, lymphamque roganti
dulce dedit, tosta quod texerat ante polenta.
sentences.l: But out of it comes an old woman, and sees the goddess, and to her asking for water gave a sweet drink, which she had covered over beforehand with toasted barley-meal.
sentences.i: But an old woman came out of it, saw the goddess, and when she asked for water gave her a sweet drink that she had covered over beforehand with toasted barley-meal.
sentences.n: 'roganti' is a participle used as a noun in the dative, 'to her asking', with 'lympham', water, as its object: Latin does not need to say 'to the goddess, who was asking'. 'dulce' is a neuter adjective used as a noun, 'something sweet' - a drink sweetened with honey. 'polenta' is barley parched and then ground, the plainest food there was, and 'texerat' means she had strewn it over the top so that it lay on the surface: that is why it will still be there when the cup is thrown. The tenses slide from present ('prodit', 'videt') to perfect ('dedit') inside the one sentence, which this poem does constantly.

sentences.t:
Dum bibit illa datum, duri puer oris et audax
constitit ante deam risitque avidamque vocavit.
sentences.l: While she is drinking what was given her, a boy of a hard face, and brazen, stood before the goddess and laughed and called her greedy.
sentences.i: While she was drinking what she had been given, a boy with a hard face and no shame planted himself in front of the goddess, laughed, and called her greedy.
sentences.n: 'datum' is a neuter participle used as a noun, 'the thing given'. 'duri oris' is a genitive of description, 'of a hard face', the Latin for barefaced or shameless - the same metaphor English keeps in 'hard-faced'. 'avidam vocavit' is 'called her greedy', with the adjective in the accusative thrown at her as a name; the contempt is the boy's own and the poem does not share it, since she has been searching without food or drink since 438. 'dum' with the present indicative again stands for past time, as at 391.

sentences.t:
Offensa est neque adhuc epota parte loquentem
cum liquido mixta perfudit diva polenta.
sentences.l: She was offended, and with the part not yet drunk up the goddess drenched him as he was speaking, with the barley-meal mixed into the liquid.
sentences.i: She took offence, and with what she had not yet drunk the goddess drenched him in mid-word, barley-meal and all.
sentences.n: 'neque adhuc epota parte' is an ablative absolute with the negative and the 'adhuc' inside it, 'the portion not yet having been drunk up': what is left in the cup is what she throws. 'loquentem' is a participle used as a noun and is the object of 'perfudit' - 'him still speaking' - so the drenching lands while his mouth is open. 'cum liquido mixta ... polenta' is an ablative of means interlaced with the rest of the line, and it matters that the barley is in it: the meal is what will stick. 'diva', the goddess, arrives late in the sentence, and the delay is the threat.

sentences.t:
Combibit os maculas, et quae modo bracchia gessit,
crura gerit; cauda est mutatis addita membris;
sentences.l: His face drank in spots, and the limbs which he lately carried as arms he carries as legs; a tail is added to his changed limbs;
sentences.i: His face drank in the spots; what he carried a moment ago as arms he now carries as legs; a tail is added to his altered limbs;
sentences.n: 'combibit os maculas' makes the face the subject and the spots the object: the skin drinks them in, so the porridge that hit him becomes his markings. 'quae modo bracchia gessit, crura gerit' puts the antecedent inside the relative clause - literally 'which limbs he lately carried as arms, he carries as legs' - and the two tenses of one verb, perfect and present, hold the before and the after inside a single line. 'mutatis membris' is a dative with 'addita', 'added to the changed limbs'.

sentences.t:
inque brevem formam, ne sit vis magna nocendi,
contrahitur, parvaque minor mensura lacerta est.
sentences.l: and he is drawn together into a small shape, so that there should not be great strength for harming, and his measure is smaller than a small lizard.
sentences.i: and he is shrunk into a small shape, so that he should not have much power to do harm, and his size is less than a small lizard's.
sentences.n: 'ne sit vis magna nocendi' is a negative purpose clause dropped inside its own sentence, between the phrase 'in brevem formam' and the verb that governs it; 'nocendi' is a gerund in the genitive, 'of harming', depending on 'vis', 'strength'. The punishment is measured deliberately: he is made small so that he can do little. 'parva ... lacerta' is an ablative of comparison, 'than a small lizard', and 'mensura' is his measure or size. 'contrahitur' is passive, and no one is named as doing it.

sentences.t:
Mirantem flentemque et tangere monstra parantem
fugit anum latebramque petit;
sentences.l: He flees the old woman, wondering and weeping and getting ready to touch the marvel, and makes for a hiding-place;
sentences.i: He flees the old woman as she wonders and weeps and reaches out to touch the marvel, and makes for a hiding-place;
sentences.n: Three accusative participles stand at the head of the sentence before the noun they agree with, 'anum', arrives at the start of the next line: the reader is given the reaction before the person, which is a standard hexameter shape and is worth waiting out rather than reordering too soon. 'fugit' takes a direct object in Latin, 'flees her', where English needs 'flees from'. 'monstra' is a neuter plural for the thing she is reaching for: a portent or marvel, a thing shown as a sign, rather than a monster in the English sense.

sentences.t:
aptumque colori
nomen habet, variis stellatus corpora guttis.
sentences.l: and he has a name suited to his colour, starred as to his body with many-coloured drops.
sentences.i: and he has a name that suits his colouring, his body starred over with mottled drops.
sentences.n: 'stellatus corpora' is a Greek accusative of respect: the participle is passive, 'starred', and the accusative names the part affected, 'as to his body'. Latin took the construction from Greek and uses it constantly with participles of this kind, and it is the one place in this part where an accusative is doing that work. The name itself is never given: it is 'stellio', the starred lizard, and the reader is left to make it out of 'stellatus' in the same line. Magnus prints 'aptum colori', 'suited to his colour'; some editions print 'pudori', 'suited to his shame', which turns the name into a verdict on the boy rather than a description of the animal.

questions: ARCHIVE DAMAGE, line 406: the archived token 'fervenu' is not a Latin word and the line does not scan as printed. Sense and metre require 'ferventia', 'boiling', agreeing with 'stagna'. Shipped unaltered, translated with a bracketed '[boiling?]', and stated plainly in the note. Needs a pipeline fix at the archive level, not a drafter's emendation.

ARCHIVE FAULT, lines 429-430: the two lines are printed in the wrong order in the archived edition - 'ossa pati flexus, ungues posuisse rigorem;' stands before 'extenuatur aquas. Molliri membra videres,', which leaves 'in illas' at the end of 428 dangling and separates 'videres' from the three infinitives it governs. The Latin Library collation flags exactly this transposition (line 429 magnus empty against latinLibrary 'extenuatur aquas molliri membra videres', and the reverse at 430). Shipped in archive order as one unit, with the translation following the order the sense requires and the note saying so. Needs a decision above drafter level.

HOUSE RENDERING CANDIDATE, 343 'Cereris sunt omnia munus': shipped as 'all things are the gift of Ceres' (literal) and 'it is all Ceres' gift' (idiomatic). Review changed the idiomatic from 'everything we have is Ceres' gift', which supplied a first-person possession the Latin has not got.
HOUSE RENDERING CANDIDATE, 391 'perpetuum ver est': shipped as 'it is spring without end' (literal) and 'it is spring the whole year round' (idiomatic).

HOUSE RENDERING CANDIDATE, 395-396 'paene simul visa est dilectaque raptaque Diti: usque adeo est properatus amor': shipped as 'almost in the same moment she was seen, and loved, and seized by Dis: so hurried was his love' (literal) and 'she was seen, loved and seized by Dis almost in one moment - his love was in that much haste' (idiomatic). Review changed the idiomatic from 'seen, desired and carried off': 'dilecta' is 'loved', not 'desired', and 'carried off' softened 'rapta' away from the literal's 'seized' at the crux line.

HOUSE RENDERING CANDIDATE, 415-416 'roganda, non rapienda fuit': shipped as 'she ought to have been asked for, not seized'. This is the moral centre of the episode and will be quoted; it should be fixed before anyone drafts the second part.

HOUSE RENDERING CANDIDATE, 416-417 'Quodsi componere magnis parva mihi fas est': shipped as 'if it is right for me to compare small things with great'. Flagged because the formula is famous in its own right and an unratified rendering here invites a later drafter to reach for a remembered one.
HOUSE RENDERING CANDIDATE, 437 'restatque nihil, quod prendere possis': shipped as 'and there remains nothing that you could take hold of'.

ADVISORY CALL: trigger 2, object form, shipped. Trigger 3 was considered for Cyane's dissolution at 427-437 and declined. It is eleven lines and it does stop and stay with a body, which is the length test; but what it describes is a body becoming water, not damage done to a body, and under the ruling that close calls go to no I left it out. If the reviewer reads the length test as decisive regardless of the kind of change, this is the place to add a second clause to the lede.

VARIANT THRESHOLD, 460: Magnus 'colori', Latin Library 'pudori'. Shipped with a clause in the note, because the two readings make the lizard's name either a description of its markings or a verdict on the boy. Confirm that is the right threshold for a one-word variant of this kind.

GRAMMAR CALL, 365 'arma manusque meae, mea, nate, potentia': taken as a string of accusatives in apposition to 'tela' at 366, the object of 'cape'. 'potentia' is formally ambiguous and could be read as a nominative in exclamation; the note says the phrase stands in apposition to 'tela' and does not name a case for it.

VARIANT, 344: Magnus 'possem' (imperfect subjunctive, an impossible wish), Latin Library 'possim' (present subjunctive, an open one). Flagged in the note as a change of mood and of force. Ignored as spelling: urget/urguet 347, siqua/si qua 378, implet/inplet 394, conlecti/collecti 399, agnovitque/adgnovitque 414, componere/conponere 416, colluerant/conluerant 447, Combibit/conbibit 455, and the 'ne c' junk at 414.

REGISTER CALL, 359 'tyrannus': rendered 'monarch', not 'tyrant'. The word names Dis by his office here, in the same breath as 'rex silentum' at 356, and there is no contempt in the Latin to carry over; under the hostile-register ruling the failure would be adding venom the Latin lacks. Flagging it because 'tyrannus' of this god will come up again.

REVIEW, 433 'membris exilibus': review took this as a dative of reference, 'for slender limbs', and rewrote the literal to match the drafter's own note, which had said dative while the literal said 'from slender limbs'. The ablative of separation is a defensible alternative reading and was what the literal originally carried; ratification should settle which reading this text ships.

REVIEW, 369-370: the repeated line-end 'numina ponti' is printed identically by both witnesses collated for this part, so review flagged no archive fault there and left the note's reading of it as deliberate repetition. If a later pass judges 370 suspect on other grounds, that note is where it should be said.

REVIEW, 429-430: the transposition the drafter reported is confirmed, against the collation and against the Latin. It is two whole lines swapped, which is a different and more serious category than the single garbled token at 406: authentic text moved rather than a word corrupted, and the reader who reads straight down the page reads a broken sentence with a stranded 'in illas'. The fix belongs at the archive level and the part ships unaltered until it is made.

REVIEW, 341: 'about' no longer names the singer or the singing-contest, because neither is in V.341-461 and the note at 344 is careful not to name them either. If the library wants that frame supplied to a reader opening the poem here, it is a policy call above drafter level.
